glosses: To make someone tired; to exhaust.
Acabar recursos o posibilidades hasta su desaparición.

examples.text: De gota en gota el agua se agota.

En el siglo XVIII, aunque la producción de azúcar no había perdido importancia, las atenciones de la Corona portuguesa se concentraron en la región donde se había descubierto oro (las Minas Gerais) el cual se agotó antes del final del siglo.

El trabajo de Darwin tuvo una influencia decisiva sobre las diferentes disciplinas científicas, y sobre el pensamiento moderno en general. Recogió su teoría en su libro El origen de las especies, publicado el 24 de noviembre de 1859 y que se agotó el primer día en que salió a la venta.
Nadie o casi nadie desea la cercanía de la muerte, pero todos saben que tarde o temprano su tiempo se agotará.

glosses: Cansar en demasía.

To cause (something) to become damaged, useless, or ineffective through continued use, especially hard, heavy, or careless use.

examples.text: You're going to wear out that game if you keep playing so rough with it.
He wears a pair of tennis shoes out every summer.

"You never take the trouble to see if he will go without it; your whip is always going as if you had the St. Vitus' dance in your arm; and if it does not wear you out, it wears your horse out; you know you are always changing your horses, and why? because you never give them any peace or encouragement."

That concertina was a wonder in its way. The handles that was on it first was wore out long ago, and he'd made new ones of braided rope yarn. And the bellows was patched in more places than a cranberry picker's overalls.

glosses: To deteriorate or become unusable or ineffective due to continued use, exposure, or strain.

examples.text: The old tractor finally wore out.
My shoes wear out quickly now that I walk to work.
Mr. Simpson adds that the station at Stanmore appears practically unchanged from the time of its opening, even to the L.N.W.R. rubber doormat, which "shows no signs of wearing out."

glosses: To exhaust; to cause or contribute to another's exhaustion, fatigue, or weariness, as by continued strain or exertion.

examples.text: You kids are wearing me out!
Trying to keep up with politics wears me out.
Our physical advantage allowed us to wear the other team out and win.

glosses: To become exhausted, tired, fatigued, or weary, as by continued strain or exertion.

examples.text: I'm wearing out, guys. Time to go to sleep.
They built our railways, but they wore themselves out in the process.

glosses: Of apparel, to display in public.

examples.text: Those sweatpants are great for loafing around the house, but they're not meant to be worn out.

glosses: Of a shirt, to not tuck into the pants; to wear in a casual manner.

examples.text: A dress shirt should be tucked in, but a t-shirt can be worn out.

glosses: To punish by spanking.
To make a mess of; to untidy, disorder, soil, or muss.

examples.text: The afternoon breeze messed up my hair.
[…] kwatumas, those aggressive and sharp-toothed eels that so thoroughly mess up one's tackle when hooked […]

glosses: To cause a problem with; to introduce an error or mistake in; to make muddled or confused; spoil; ruin.

examples.text: The change messed something up, and it's not working anymore.

glosses: To botch, bungle; to perform poorly on.

examples.text: Well, I messed up my solo, but otherwise it was a good concert.

glosses: To make a mistake; to do something incorrectly; to perform poorly.

examples.text: She messed up on her final exam.
He has a hard time getting started because he's afraid he'll mess up.

glosses: To cause (another person) to make unwanted mistakes in a given task, usually through distraction or obnoxious behavior.

examples.text: Stop bumping me! You keep messing me up!

glosses: To damage; injure.

examples.text: He messed up his elbow at the track meet.

glosses: To manhandle; beat up; rough up.

examples.text: Her brother's friends messed him up a little after he cheated on her.

glosses: To discombobulate, utterly confuse, or confound psychologically; to throw into a state of mental disarray.

examples.text: That girl totally messed me up, man. I'm not sure who I am anymore.

glosses: The remains of a destroyed or dilapidated construction, such as a house or castle.

examples.text: The Veian and the Gabian towirs shall fall, / And one promiscuous ruin cover all; / Nor, after length of years, a stone betray / The place where once the very ruins lay.

glosses: The state of being a ruin, destroyed or decayed.

examples.text: The monastery has fallen into ruin.

glosses: Something that leads to serious trouble or destruction.

examples.text: Gambling has been the ruin of many.

glosses: The act of ruining something.

the ruin of a constitution or a government

examples.text: With all these purchases, you surely mean to ruin us!

glosses: To destroy or render something no longer usable or operable.

examples.text: He ruined his new white slacks by accidentally spilling oil on them.

glosses: To upset or overturn the plans or progress of, or to have a disastrous effect on something.

examples.text: My car breaking down just as I was on the road ruined my vacation.

glosses: To make something less enjoyable or likeable.

examples.text: I used to love that song, but being assaulted when that song was playing ruined the song for me.

glosses: To reveal the ending of (a story); to spoil.
